implementation_notes: Boost.Asio documents itself as an implementation of this pattern: io_context is the Proactor, completion handlers are function objects, and the asynchronous operation processor is the operating system on Windows (overlapped I/O and I/O completion ports) or a reactor over select/epoll/kqueue elsewhere. The handler factory and the service roles collapse into completion handlers that initiate the next operation, so the classic structure survives mainly as the initiator and handler convention.
pitfalls: A single-threaded io_context must not run blocking work inside a completion handler; any blocking call serialises every other completion.

Handler state (sockets, buffers, timers) can outlive the initiating scope: use shared ownership or a strand, and remember that cancelling an operation still invokes its handler with operation_aborted.

variants.name: Boost.Asio with C++20 coroutines
variants.idiom_name: co_await async_* with use_awaitable or co_spawn
variants.implementation_notes: C++20 stackless coroutines turn the callback chain into linear code: the completion handler becomes the resumption of the coroutine and errors surface as exceptions unless as_tuple or redirect_error is used. Prefer it where the toolchain is C++20 and the callback pyramid hurts readability; the roles and the io_context remain the same.
pitfalls: Detached co_spawn erases ownership: the coroutine must own the objects it references; a coroutine resumed after its connection object died is the coroutine-era analogue of the dangling-buffer bug.
Without as_tuple or redirect_error the error_code becomes a thrown system_error, silently changing the error-handling style of the surrounding code.

variants.name: ACE_Proactor and ACE_Asynch_Acceptor (classic)
variants.implementation_notes: The pattern's classic home: ACE ships ACE_Proactor, ACE_Asynch_Acceptor and handler skeletons that wrap I/O completion ports on Windows and POSIX aio elsewhere, with the Reactor as the fallback demultiplexer, exactly as POSA2 describes it. Choose it only when ACE's service-configuration and policy layers are already in the stack; otherwise Boost.Asio is the smaller dependency.
pitfalls: ACE couples handlers to its Reactor and Service Configurator machinery and to its own build system; adopting it for this pattern alone is rarely justified.
